nodes.definition: Pearl's first rung: seeing. P(Y|T) — passive observation. Conditional probabilities, correlation, regression. Cannot distinguish causation from confounding.
nodes.name: Rung 1 — Association

nodes.definition: Pearl's second rung: doing. P(Y|do(T)) — external manipulation, graph surgery. Answers 'what happens if we force T?' Requires causal assumptions (DAG).
nodes.name: Rung 2 — Intervention

nodes.definition: Pearl's third rung: imagining. P(Y(0)=0 | T=1, Y=1) — same unit, different treatment. Requires the full SCM with noise structure. Answers 'was it the treatment that caused THIS outcome?'
nodes.name: Rung 3 — Counterfactuals

nodes.definition: P(A) = sum_i P(A | B_i) P(B_i) for a partition {B_i}. The foundation of adjustment formulas, stratification, and g-computation.
nodes.name: Law of Total Probability

nodes.definition: P(H|D) = P(D|H)P(H)/P(D). Updates prior beliefs with evidence. The engine of Bayesian inference, posterior computation, and abduction (rung 3 counterfactuals).
nodes.name: Bayes' Rule

nodes.definition: The sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches N(mu, sigma^2/n) as n increases, regardless of the population distribution (under finite variance). Justifies normal-approximation CIs.
nodes.name: Central Limit Theorem

nodes.definition: Choose parameters that maximize the probability of observing the data. MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal, and efficient under regularity conditions. Foundation of most statistical modeling.
nodes.name: Maximum Likelihood Estimation

nodes.definition: MSE = Bias^2 + Variance + irreducible error. Regularization reduces variance at the cost of increased bias. In causal inference, regularization bias in nuisance models can contaminate the causal estimand (the nD trap).
nodes.name: Bias-Variance Tradeoff

nodes.definition: Adding a penalty term to the loss function (L1/L2/elastic net) to constrain model complexity. Prevents overfitting but introduces bias. In causal ML, this bias must be removed by orthogonal scores (DML) or targeting (TMLE).
nodes.name: Regularization

nodes.definition: Splitting data into folds for honest model evaluation. In causal inference, cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al. 2018) uses held-out folds to prevent overfitting bias from contaminating causal estimates.
nodes.name: Cross-Validation

nodes.definition: An interval [L, U] that covers the true parameter with probability 1-alpha over repeated sampling. In causal inference, the CI quantifies sampling uncertainty but NOT model/graph uncertainty.
nodes.name: Confidence Interval

nodes.definition: The probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one computed, under the null hypothesis. In causal inference, refutation tests use p-values from placebo/randomization distributions, not from regression tables.
nodes.name: P-value

nodes.definition: Rejecting a true null hypothesis. In causal refutation, a placebo test that falsely rejects the null (tau=0) is a type I error — the pipeline claims an effect where none exists.
nodes.name: Type I Error (False Positive)

nodes.definition: Probability of correctly rejecting a false null. In causal inference, power calculations determine minimum detectable effect sizes and sample size requirements for planned studies.
nodes.name: Statistical Power

nodes.definition: The coefficient on X in a regression of Y on X and Z equals the coefficient from regressing Y (residualized on Z) on X (residualized on Z). Shows that regression 'partials out' controls — the math behind linear adjustment.
nodes.formal_def: \hat{\beta}_X = (X^\top M_Z X)^{-1} X^\top M_Z Y, \; M_Z = I - Z(Z^\top Z)^{-1}Z^\top
nodes.name: Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem

nodes.definition: A node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents. The bridge between graph structure and probability: the joint distribution factorizes according to the DAG.
nodes.formal_def: X \perp NonDescendants(X) \mid pa(X) \Rightarrow P(V) = \prod_j P(V_j \mid pa(V_j))
nodes.name: Markov Condition

nodes.definition: The treated and untreated groups are comparable in their potential outcomes. In randomized experiments, exchangeability holds by design. In observational studies, it requires the ignorability assumption.
nodes.name: Exchangeability

nodes.definition: Y = T*Y(1) + (1-T)*Y(0): the observed outcome equals the potential outcome under the treatment actually received. Links counterfactual notation to observed data. Part of SUTVA.
nodes.name: Consistency Assumption

nodes.definition: Hume (1748): causation is constant conjunction — we observe regular succession, not necessary connection. The original articulation of the problem that causal inference tries to solve. 'We never observe causes — only regularities.'
nodes.name: Humean Causation

nodes.definition: Lewis (1973): 'X causes Y' means 'Y would not have occurred if X had not occurred' in the closest possible world. The philosophical foundation of the potential outcomes framework.
nodes.formal_def: X \text{ causes } Y \iff Y(\neg X) \neq Y(X) \text{ in the closest world}
nodes.name: Counterfactual Theory of Causation

nodes.definition: Woodward (2003): X causes Y if intervening on X (while holding everything else fixed) changes Y. The philosophical foundation of Pearl's do-operator and the interventionist account of causation.
nodes.name: Manipulability Theory

nodes.definition: Cartwright (1999): 'No causes in, no causes out.' A causal model is only as good as the causal knowledge that went into it. Data alone, without causal assumptions, cannot produce causal conclusions.
nodes.name: Cartwright's Dictum

nodes.definition: Bias from non-random selection into treatment: treated units differ systematically from untreated units in ways that affect outcomes. The econometric formulation of confounding (Heckman 1979).
nodes.formal_def: E[Y\mid T=1] - E[Y\mid T=0] = ATE + \underbrace{E[Y(0)\mid T=1] - E[Y(0)\mid T=0]}_{\text{selection bias}}
nodes.name: Heckman Selection Bias

nodes.definition: X 'Granger-causes' Y if past values of X improve prediction of Y beyond past values of Y alone. Important: Granger causality is predictive, not causal — it does not imply X causes Y in the interventionist sense.
nodes.name: Granger Causality

nodes.definition: Fixed effects, random effects, and difference-in-differences exploit panel structure to control for unobserved time-invariant confounders. DiD is the workhorse causal method in econometrics.
nodes.name: Panel Data Methods

nodes.definition: Nine criteria for assessing causality from observational evidence (Hill 1965): strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy. Pre-cursor to modern causal formalization but still widely taught.
nodes.name: Bradford Hill Criteria

nodes.definition: Hernan & Robins (2016): specify the idealized RCT you would run, then emulate it from observational data. Prevents method-driven analysis. The foundation of modern causal epidemiology.
nodes.name: Target Trial Emulation

nodes.definition: A confounder must be (1) associated with exposure, (2) associated with outcome, (3) not on the causal path. Greenland, Pearl & Robins (1999) unified the epidemiological definition with the graphical one.
nodes.name: Confounding in Epidemiology

nodes.definition: Learning representations that capture causal structure rather than mere statistical associations. Scholkopf et al. (2021): the next frontier for robust, generalizable, fair ML systems.
nodes.name: Causal Representation Learning

nodes.definition: RL agents that learn causal models of their environment to plan interventions and generalize across tasks. Combines Pearl's causal hierarchy with Sutton's RL framework. Active research area.
nodes.name: Causal Reinforcement Learning

nodes.definition: Causal definitions of fairness (counterfactual fairness, no unresolved discrimination) require causal models. Associational fairness criteria can be mutually inconsistent and fail to address root causes of bias.
nodes.name: Fairness in Machine Learning

nodes.definition: Campbell & Stanley (1963): internal validity (is the effect causal?), external validity (does it generalize?), construct validity (are we measuring what we think?), statistical conclusion validity. The social-science precursor to modern causal design.
nodes.name: Campbell's Validity Framework

nodes.definition: Baron & Kenny (1986): the classic regression-based approach to mediation analysis. Modern causal mediation (VanderWeele, Imai, Pearl) generalizes this to allow interactions, nonlinearities, and identification from DAGs rather than regression coefficients.
nodes.name: Mediation in Psychology

nodes.definition: Research designs that approximate randomized experiments when randomization is infeasible: regression discontinuity, interrupted time series, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables. Shadish, Cook & Campbell (2002) is the canonical reference.
nodes.name: Quasi-Experiments

nodes.definition: Robins' generalized methods for time-varying confounding: g-computation (parametric), IPTW (weighting), g-estimation (structural nested models). The biostatistics foundation of modern longitudinal causal inference.
nodes.name: G-Methods

nodes.definition: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983): e(X) = P(T=1|X). The propensity score is a balancing score — conditioning on e(X) is sufficient to remove confounding. Reduces high-dimensional X to a scalar, enabling matching, stratification, and IPW.
nodes.name: Propensity Score

nodes.definition: Rosenbaum (2002): bounding the treatment effect under hypothetical unmeasured confounding. The E-value (VanderWeele & Ding 2017) is the modern, standardized version used throughout this project.
nodes.name: Sensitivity Analysis in Epidemiology

nodes.definition: P(prediction | data) = integral of P(prediction | theta) * P(theta | data) d-theta. The Bayesian engine for integrating out nuisance parameters. Structurally identical to causal adjustment (Sigma) but operates on P(Z|T) rather than P(Z) — conditions instead of intervening.
nodes.formal_def: P(\tilde{y} \mid D) = \int P(\tilde{y} \mid \theta) P(\theta \mid D) d\theta
nodes.name: Bayesian Marginalization

nodes.definition: Conditioning (Bayes): P(Y | T) = sum_z P(Y | T, z) P(z | T). Intervening (causal): P(Y | do(T)) = sum_z P(Y | T, z) P(z). Same Sigma, different weight. The difference between Rung 1 and Rung 2 is entirely in whether you use P(z|T) or P(z).
nodes.name: Conditioning vs. Intervening

nodes.definition: Pearl's formal definition of intervention: delete P(T|pa(T)) from the Markov factorization, fix T=t. P(V|do(T=t)) = prod_{Vj≠T} P(Vj | pa(Vj)) |_{T=t}. The general mechanism from which all identification formulas (back-door, front-door, IV) are derived by marginalizing over subsets of variables.
nodes.name: Truncated Factorization

nodes.definition: A complete polynomial-time algorithm that determines whether any causal effect is identifiable from a given DAG and, if so, expresses it as a sequence of Sigma (marginalization) operations over observed variables. Every identifiable causal effect is a Sigma expression.
nodes.name: ID Algorithm (Shpitser & Pearl 2006)

nodes.definition: E[Y(1) − Y(0)]: the expected difference in outcomes if everyone vs. no one received treatment.
nodes.name: Average Treatment Effect (ATE)

nodes.definition: ATE conditioned on covariates: E[Y(1)−Y(0) | X=x]. Captures treatment effect heterogeneity.
nodes.name: Conditional ATE (CATE)

nodes.definition: ATE for compliers in an IV design. Identified when the instrument satisfies relevance, exclusion, and independence.
nodes.name: Local ATE (LATE)

nodes.definition: A set Z satisfies the back-door criterion relative to (T,Y) if no node in Z is a descendant of T, and Z d-separates T from Y in the back-door graph (Pearl 1995, Def. 3.3.1).
nodes.name: Back-Door Criterion

nodes.definition: Identifies the ATE when a mediator M intercepts all causal paths from T to Y and shares no confounders with Y. More fragile than back-door (requires no T→Y direct edge).
nodes.formal_def: T \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y, T \perp Y \mid do(M)
nodes.name: Front-Door Criterion

nodes.definition: Three rules (R1–R3) that transform expressions involving the do-operator into observational quantities. Complete for identifying any identifiable causal effect (Shpitser & Pearl 2006).
nodes.formal_def: R1: P(y\mid do(x),z,w)=P(y\mid do(x),w)\text{ if }Y\perp Z\mid X,W\text{ in }G_{\bar{X}}
nodes.name: do-Calculus

nodes.definition: Graphical test for conditional independence: a path is blocked if it contains a chain/fork with the middle node conditioned on, or a collider with neither the collider nor any descendant conditioned on.
nodes.name: d-Separation

nodes.definition: A common cause of T and Y that creates spurious association. Without adjustment for confounders, P(Y|T) ≠ P(Y|do(T)).
nodes.name: Confounding

nodes.definition: Conditioning on a common effect of T and Y opens a spurious path, creating association where none exists. Never condition on a collider or its descendants.
nodes.formal_def: T\rightarrow S\leftarrow Y, \text{ condition on }S\Rightarrow T\not\perp Y
nodes.name: Collider Bias (Berkson's Paradox)

nodes.definition: A variable M on the causal path from T to Y (T→M→Y). Adjusting for M blocks the indirect effect — only appropriate when estimating the direct effect.
nodes.name: Mediation

nodes.definition: Z affects T (relevance), has no direct effect on Y except through T (exclusion), and is independent of confounders. Identifies LATE for compliers.
nodes.formal_def: Z\rightarrow T, Z\not\rightarrow Y, Z\perp U
nodes.name: Instrumental Variable (IV)

nodes.definition: A variable that shares the same confounders as the outcome but has no causal effect from treatment. A non-zero estimated T→NC effect signals residual confounding (Lipsitch et al. 2010).
nodes.name: Negative Control

nodes.definition: Quantifies how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to explain away an observed effect. The E-value (VanderWeele & Ding 2017) is the most widely used metric.
nodes.name: Sensitivity Analysis

nodes.definition: Every unit must have non-zero probability of receiving either treatment: 0 < P(T=1|X=x) < 1 for all x. Without it, ATE requires extrapolation.
nodes.name: Positivity (Overlap)

nodes.definition: {Y(0),Y(1)} independent of T given X: all common causes of T and Y are measured and adjusted for. Fundamentally untestable from observational data.
nodes.name: Ignorability (Unconfoundedness)

nodes.definition: Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption: (1) no interference between units, (2) consistency — the observed Y equals the potential outcome under the treatment actually received.
nodes.name: SUTVA

nodes.definition: The derivative of the expected score with respect to nuisance parameters is zero at the true values. First-order errors in nuisance models cancel out rather than contaminating the causal estimand (Chernozhukov et al. 2018).
nodes.name: Neyman Orthogonality

nodes.definition: An estimator is doubly robust if it is consistent when EITHER the propensity model OR the outcome model is correctly specified — not both. AIPW and TMLE are doubly robust.
nodes.name: Double Robustness

nodes.definition: A correctly specified causal mechanism P(effect | direct causes) is invariant across environments (Peters, Buhlmann & Meinshausen 2016). Used for causal discovery and drift detection.
nodes.name: Invariance Principle

nodes.definition: An association that appears in aggregated data reverses or disappears within subgroups. The data alone cannot tell you whether to condition — that decision requires causal knowledge (which variable is the confounder?).
nodes.name: Simpson's Paradox

nodes.description: Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting: doubly-robust, Neyman-orthogonal estimator using cross-fit gradient boosting for nuisances.
nodes.name: AIPW

nodes.description: Orthogonal scores + cross-fitting to debias ML nuisance estimates. Achieves sqrt(n)-consistency with data-adaptive nuisances (Chernozhukov et al. 2018).
nodes.name: Double/Debiased ML

nodes.description: Weights observations by inverse propensity score to create a pseudo-population where treatment is independent of covariates.
nodes.name: Inverse Probability Weighting

nodes.description: Targets the estimand by fluctuating initial nuisance estimates. Doubly robust and locally efficient (van der Laan & Rose 2011).
nodes.name: Targeted Maximum Likelihood

nodes.description: Constraint-based causal discovery: tests conditional independencies, removes edges, orients colliders. Returns Markov equivalence class. Assumes causal sufficiency (no latent confounders).
nodes.name: PC Algorithm

nodes.description: Fast Causal Inference: extends PC to allow arbitrary latent confounders. Returns a Partial Ancestral Graph (PAG). More conservative but more honest than PC.
nodes.name: FCI Algorithm

nodes.description: Score-based causal discovery: greedily adds/removes edges to maximize BIC. Returns the highest-scoring Markov equivalence class.
nodes.name: Greedy Equivalence Search

nodes.question: What causal structure do we believe?

nodes.name: IDENTIFY
nodes.question: Can the effect be computed from observables?

nodes.name: FEATURE
nodes.question: What enters the model — and what must not?

nodes.name: EVOLVE
nodes.question: Is the world still the one we modeled?

nodes.result: LATE on ED visits and depression (Finkelstein et al. 2012)

nodes.name: Sachs Protein Signaling
nodes.result: 24 edges recovered vs 16 interventional ground truth

nodes.name: Assumptions Are First-Class Artifacts
nodes.statement: Every causal claim carries a versioned, inspectable assumption object (DAG + SCM). No claim without its assumptions.

nodes.name: Graph = Single Source of Truth
nodes.statement: Identification, adjustment sets, test suites, and monitoring checks are compiled from the DAG, not hand-maintained.

nodes.name: Sensors + Actuators at Every Stage
nodes.statement: Each station emits quantitative health signals and has defined revision actions — the loop is closeable.

nodes.name: Refutation Is Continuous
nodes.statement: Placebo tests, negative controls, and falsification checks run in CI and production monitoring, not once at publication.

nodes.name: Ground Truth Where Possible
nodes.statement: Development happens against synthetic DGPs with known effects; methods graduate to real data only after passing synthetic acceptance tests.

nodes.name: Ladder Discipline
nodes.statement: Every query is labeled by its rung on Pearl's ladder; rung-2/3 questions with rung-1 machinery require recorded assumptions.

nodes.insight: The data alone cannot tell you whether to condition on 'city' — that decision is causal.
nodes.limitation: Cannot distinguish confounding from causation; rung 1 only.
nodes.name: Foundations

nodes.insight: Bayesian inference updates beliefs about parameters of a fixed observational model — it never leaves rung 1 by itself.
nodes.limitation: Perfect posterior concentrates on the wrong causal effect under confounding.
nodes.name: Bayesian Inference

nodes.insight: A BN is a joint distribution with a graph; nothing in it yet says 'cause' — any orientation in the Markov equivalence class fits equally well.
nodes.limitation: Markov equivalence: cannot distinguish X→Y from X←Y without additional assumptions.
nodes.name: Bayesian Networks
nodes.topic: d-separation, Markov condition, structure learning (PC, GES)

nodes.insight: do() differs from condition(): P(Y|T) ≠ P(Y|do(T)) exactly by confounding. Front-door criterion applied without checking fails silently.
nodes.limitation: Requires full SCM for counterfactuals (rung 3); DAG alone only reaches rung 2.
nodes.name: The Causal Step

nodes.insight: Identification is exact and assumption-driven; estimation is approximate and data-driven — the two error budgets must never be conflated.
nodes.limitation: nD trap: Lasso plug-in bias 0.39 vs DML 0.04; regularization bias contaminates causal estimates in high dimensions.
nodes.name: Estimation Theory
nodes.topic: AIPW, DML, double robustness, Neyman orthogonality

nodes.insight: The back-door criterion is a theorem about the diagram, not an axiom — it can be re-derived as wire surgery in categorical probability.
nodes.limitation: Requires abstract algebra; pedagogical bridge, not a practical tool.
nodes.name: Compositional Capstone
